memories.content: Avoid em dashes in the proposal; split the sentence or use more ordinary punctuation instead.
The user tends to place several independently reviewable claims in one long sentence.
Use first-person active voice for choices and commitments owned by the proposal author so responsibility remains explicit throughout the work plan.
Describe prototype operations that have already been implemented and verified as observed states.
Describe prototype operations not yet implemented or evaluated as plans or expectations.
When a commitment is phrased passively, readers may interpret it as uncertainty, evasiveness, or reluctance to take responsibility.
Use “we” only for decisions and commitments the authors control, not for external facts or actions owned by another party.
The user should use one first-person pronoun consistently for the same authorial role and should not alternate between “I” and “we” unless the responsible party actually changes.
The user tends to hide unsettled commitments behind passive phrases such as “will be considered” or “is expected.”
Split proposal prose into short sentences when a sentence contains more than one independently reviewable claim.
Keep one main claim in each sentence so a reviewer can locate and assess it quickly.
The user tends to repeat em dashes when a sentence already contains several clauses.
Repeated em dashes can shift a reviewer’s attention from the proposal’s argument to suspicion that its prose was generated by AI.
List whom to notify and in what order if serious discomfort is reported during the study.
Field staff rely on the pre-defined contact sequence when serious discomfort is reported.
Define the thresholds for participant harm, operational disruption, and data anomalies at which deployment and data collection must cease.
Establish procedures to restore existing systems and workflow states after suspending field deployment.
The user's stop plan can be judged feasible only when it identifies who has authority to order recovery and who is responsible for carrying it out.

In organizations where error reporting is linked to individual performance evaluations, safety signal records may be separated from research decision logs, potentially breaking the traceability path for the same incident.

analysis.overview: The frames address separate domains. The reference frame concerns proposal prose, authorial responsibility, and evidentiary status, while the compared frame concerns field-study escalation, stopping, recovery, and incident traceability. Neither frame supplies a scope-aligned counterpart to the other’s operational claims.

reports.compared_only: The compared frame uniquely specifies discomfort escalation, stop thresholds, system recovery planning and ownership, and protection of incident traceability across organizational records.
reports.reference_only: The reference uniquely promotes atomic sentences, restrained punctuation, explicit authorial responsibility, stable pronoun roles, and status-accurate descriptions of prototype operations.
